content: Dental plaque-induced gingivitis is a reversible inflammatory condition caused by the accumulation and persistence of microbial biofilms, commonly referred to as dental plaque, on the teeth. This condition is characterized by redness, swelling, and an increased tendency for the gums (gingivae) to bleed easily. In individuals who are susceptible, untreated gingivitis can progress to periodontitis, which involves the destruction of the soft tissue and bone that support the teeth. Chlorhexidine mouthrinse is hypothesized to reduce plaque accumulation, thereby mitigating gingivitis. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate the effectiveness of chlorhexidine mouthrinse as an adjunct to mechanical oral hygiene practices, such as toothbrushing with or without dental floss or interdental cleaning aids, in controlling gingivitis and plaque. Comparisons were made between chlorhexidine mouthrinse and either mechanical oral hygiene alone or mechanical oral hygiene combined with a placebo or control mouthrinse. The study also aimed to assess whether the concentration of chlorhexidine or the frequency of rinsing (once daily versus twice daily) influenced its effectiveness. Additionally, adverse effects associated with the use of chlorhexidine mouthrinse were documented. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Oral Health Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and CINAHL, up to September 28, 2016. They also searched ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform for ongoing trials. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date during the search. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) were included if they evaluated the effects of chlorhexidine mouthrinse used for at least four weeks as an adjunct to mechanical oral hygiene in children and adults. Participants could have gingivitis, periodontitis, or be otherwise healthy, including those with medical conditions or special care needs. Mechanical oral hygiene practices included toothbrushing with or without flossing or interdental cleaning aids, and could also involve professional tooth cleaning or periodontal treatment. Two independent reviewers screened the search results, extracted data, and assessed the risk of bias in the included studies. For continuous outcomes, mean differences (MD) and standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated. For dichotomous outcomes, risk ratios (RR) with 95% CIs were reported. Random-effects models were used for all meta-analyses due to anticipated heterogeneity. A total of 51 studies involving 5,345 participants were included. One study was assessed as having an unclear risk of bias, while the remaining 50 studies were deemed to have a high risk of bias. However, the quality of evidence for gingivitis and plaque outcomes was considered high, as further research was unlikely to change the confidence in the effect estimates. Gingivitis: After 4 to 6 weeks of use, chlorhexidine mouthrinse reduced gingivitis, as measured by the Gingival Index (GI) on a 0 to 3 scale, by 0.21 (95% CI 0.11 to 0.31) compared to placebo, control, or no mouthrinse. This analysis included 10 trials with 805 participants who had mild gingival inflammation (mean GI score of 1). A similar reduction in gingivitis was observed at six months. However, there were insufficient data to determine the effect of chlorhexidine mouthrinse on individuals with moderate or severe gingival inflammation (mean GI scores of 1.1 to 3). Plaque: Plaque levels were assessed using various indices. At 4 to 6 weeks, the SMD for plaque reduction was 1.45 (95% CI 1.00 to 1.90) standard deviations lower in the chlorhexidine group compared to controls, indicating a substantial reduction in plaque. This analysis included 12 trials with 950 participants. A similarly large reduction in plaque was observed at six months. Extrinsic Tooth Staining: Participants using chlorhexidine mouthrinse experienced a significant increase in extrinsic tooth staining at 4 to 6 weeks. The SMD for staining was 1.07 (95% CI 0.80 to 1.34) standard deviations higher in the chlorhexidine group compared to controls. This finding was based on eight trials involving 415 participants. Increased staining was also observed at 7 to 12 weeks and at six months. Calculus Formation: The effect of chlorhexidine mouthrinse on calculus formation was inconclusive due to insufficient data. Effect of Concentration and Frequency of Rinsing: There was insufficient evidence to determine whether the concentration of chlorhexidine or the frequency of rinsing (once daily versus twice daily) influenced its effectiveness. Other Adverse Effects: The most commonly reported adverse effects included taste disturbances or alterations (reported in 11 studies), oral mucosal effects such as soreness, irritation, mild desquamation, and mucosal ulceration or erosions (reported in 13 studies), and a general burning sensation or burning tongue (reported in nine studies). Conclusions: High-quality evidence indicates that chlorhexidine mouthrinse reduces gingivitis in individuals with mild gingival inflammation, but the reduction is not considered clinically significant. There is also high-quality evidence of a substantial reduction in dental plaque when chlorhexidine mouthrinse is used as an adjunct to mechanical oral hygiene for 4 to 6 weeks and up to six months. However, there is no evidence to suggest that one concentration of chlorhexidine is more effective than another. Insufficient evidence exists to determine the effect of chlorhexidine mouthrinse on moderate or severe gingival inflammation. Prolonged use of chlorhexidine mouthrinse (four weeks or longer) is associated with extrinsic tooth staining and other adverse effects, including taste disturbances, oral mucosal irritation, and a burning sensation.
